did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to David and states that it was written when the Philistines seized him in Gath.
Did you know? The psalm opens with a plea for mercy: the psalmist describes the continual pressure from other people and turns to God for help.
Did you know? Even when the psalmist declares that he is afraid, he immediately emphasizes his choice to trust in God: “When I am afraid, I will trust in you.”
Did you know? Trust in God leads the psalmist to say that he is not afraid of what human beings can do to him.
Did you know? The psalmist’s enemies do more than oppress him; according to the psalm, they also distress him with their words and set their thoughts on evil.
Did you know? The enemies are described as hiding, watching the psalmist’s steps, and keeping track of his movements in order to harm him.
Did you know? The psalmist presents his wanderings and tears as details that God knows and remembers: “You have kept count of my wanderings” and “Put my tears in your bottle.”
Did you know? The psalmist connects his calling on God with the retreat of his enemies and summarizes it with this clear declaration: “This I know: God is for me.”
Did you know? In verses 11–12, the psalm repeats twice that God is praised and trusted, emphasizing the central place of faith amid danger.
Did you know? The psalm ends by describing deliverance from death and from falling, so that the psalmist can continue to walk before God “in the light of life.”
